blocks.text: Cellular respiration is the universal process by which organisms break down complex carbon-containing compounds such as glucose to get usable energy: C6H12O6 + 6O2 gives 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy. The arrangement of atoms in glucose has more stored energy, and the arrangement in CO2 and H2O much less, because glucose has many C-H bonds while CO2 and H2O have none.

blocks.title: External and cellular respiration
blocks.text: The exchange of CO2 and O2 between an organism and its environment is external respiration, or breathing. Cellular respiration is the process by which energy is made available to cells by the step-by-step oxidation of food inside them.

The basic events of cellular respiration are much the same in all cells, and almost all cells in all organisms use glucose as their energy source; that is why glucose is known as the respiratory fuel. Many of the reactions in your cells also occur in the cells of frogs, mice, planaria, mushrooms and radishes. There are two main types: anaerobic respiration (fermentation), in the absence of oxygen, and aerobic respiration, in the presence of oxygen. In the first step of both, glucose is split into two molecules of pyruvic acid (C3H4O3) in glycolysis; the later reactions of pyruvic acid differ.
Mechanism of anaerobic respiration

Anaerobic respiration happens in many microorganisms, in some cells of higher plants and in the muscle cells of vertebrates. Glucose is not completely oxidised, so this type of respiration yields relatively little energy: one glucose molecule gives only two ATPs, about 2 percent of the energy in glucose, equivalent to 14.6 kcal. Anaerobic respiration consists of glycolysis followed by the reduction of pyruvic acid by NADH to either lactic acid or alcohol and CO2.

items: Alcoholic fermentation: in primitive prokaryotic cells (bacteria) and in some eukaryotic cells such as yeast, pyruvic acid is further broken down into alcohol (C2H5OH) and CO2: 2 C3H4O3 gives 2 C2H5OH + 2 CO2.

Lactic acid fermentation: each pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid (C3H6O3) in the absence of oxygen: 2 C3H4O3 gives 2 C3H6O3. This occurs in the muscle cells of humans and other animals during extreme physical activity, when oxygen cannot be transported to the cells as fast as it is needed; many bacteria also use it.

blocks.alt: Two flow charts. Left, alcoholic fermentation: glucose to two pyruvic acids by glycolysis, then to two ethanol plus two carbon dioxide. Right, lactic acid fermentation: glucose to two pyruvic acids, then to two lactic acids with no carbon dioxide.
blocks.caption: Alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation (original diagram after Figure 5.13 of the chapter).
blocks.long_description: Both begin with glycolysis, which gives two pyruvic acids, two ATP and two NADH. In alcoholic fermentation (bacteria, yeast) each pyruvic acid loses CO2 and is reduced by NADH to ethanol. In lactic acid fermentation (muscle in hard exercise, many bacteria) each pyruvic acid is reduced directly to lactic acid with no CO2. Either way the NAD+ is regenerated so glycolysis can continue, but only two ATP per glucose are gained.

blocks.text: Mechanism of aerobic respiration

The complete breakdown of glucose occurs only in aerobic respiration: glucose is broken down to pyruvic acid, which is then completely oxidised to CO2 and water, and all the energy stored in its C-H bonds is released. Cellular respiration is a continuous process, but for study it is divided into four stages: glycolysis, pyruvic acid oxidation, the Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle), and the electron transport chain with chemiosmosis. Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol and does not need oxygen; the other three stages occur in the mitochondria, where oxygen is essential.

blocks.title: When oxygen was scarce
blocks.text: When life evolved on Earth free oxygen was not available, so only anaerobic respiration was possible. With the evolution of photosynthesis, molecular oxygen slowly accumulated in the atmosphere, and the presence of free oxygen made the evolution of aerobic respiration possible.

blocks.alt: A blue cytosol box on the left, where glucose becomes pyruvic acid by glycolysis, with a grey branch to the anaerobic products. An orange mitochondrion on the right, where pyruvic acid becomes acetyl-CoA, enters the Krebs cycle and feeds the electron transport chain, which takes in oxygen and releases water.
blocks.caption: Overview of cellular respiration (original diagram after Figure 5.14 of the chapter).
blocks.long_description: Glycolysis in the cytosol splits glucose into pyruvic acid without needing oxygen; without oxygen the pyruvic acid is fermented to lactic acid or ethanol and CO2. With oxygen the pyruvic acid enters the mitochondrion, is oxidised to acetyl-CoA, passes through the Krebs cycle, which releases CO2 and loads NADH and FADH2, and these feed the electron transport chain, where chemiosmosis makes most of the ATP and oxygen is reduced to water.

blocks.text: Stage 1: glycolysis

Glycolysis is the breakdown of glucose into two molecules of pyruvic acid. It occurs in both anaerobic and aerobic respiration, in a series of steps each catalysed by a specific enzyme dissolved in the cytosol; ATP and the coenzyme NAD+ are also essential. It has a preparatory phase and an oxidative phase.
Preparatory phase
This phase spends energy and breaks glucose.

items: A phosphate group is transferred from ATP to glucose, which becomes glucose 6-phosphate.
Glucose 6-phosphate is converted into its isomer fructose 6-phosphate.
Another ATP transfers a second phosphate group to fructose 6-phosphate, which becomes fructose 1,6-biphosphate.

Fructose 1,6-biphosphate is highly reactive and breaks into two three-carbon intermediates, glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (G3P) and dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DAP). These interconvert, giving two molecules of G3P.

blocks.text: Oxidative phase
This phase removes hydrogen from G3P and packs the released energy as ATP; each step happens twice, once for each G3P.

items: Each G3P is oxidised to its acidic form: two hydrogen atoms (with two high-energy electrons) are removed and transferred to NAD+, and an inorganic phosphate is added, giving 1,3-biphosphoglyceric acid (1,3-BPGA).
A phosphate group is transferred from 1,3-BPGA to ADP, giving 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA) and a molecule of ATP.
3-PGA is converted to 2-phosphoglyceric acid (2-PGA).
2-PGA is dehydrated (water removed) to phosphoenol pyruvic acid (PEP).
PEP gives up its high-energy phosphate to convert a second ADP to ATP, and becomes pyruvic acid.

blocks.alt: A vertical flow chart from glucose at the top to two pyruvic acids at the bottom. The green preparatory phase spends two ATP to make glucose 6-phosphate, fructose 6-phosphate and fructose 1,6-biphosphate, which splits into G3P and dihydroxyacetone phosphate. The purple oxidative phase turns two G3P into 1,3-biphosphoglyceric acid (two NADH), 3-phosphoglyceric acid (two ATP), 2-phosphoglyceric acid, phosphoenol pyruvic acid and pyruvic acid (two ATP).
blocks.caption: The steps of glycolysis (original diagram after Figure 5.15 of the chapter).
blocks.long_description: In the preparatory phase two ATP are spent: glucose is phosphorylated to glucose 6-phosphate, isomerised to fructose 6-phosphate, phosphorylated again to fructose 1,6-biphosphate, and split into G3P and DAP, which becomes a second G3P. In the oxidative phase each G3P is oxidised and phosphorylated to 1,3-biphosphoglyceric acid, reducing NAD+ to NADH; its phosphate goes to ADP, giving 3-phosphoglyceric acid and ATP; this becomes 2-phosphoglyceric acid, loses water to form PEP, and PEP gives its phosphate to ADP to make ATP and pyruvic acid. Net: 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose.

blocks.title: Glucose in and out
blocks.text: Glucose enters cells from the tissue fluid by passive transport through a specific glucose carrier, which can be gated by hormones such as insulin. Pyruvic acid can also be turned back into glucose by reversing glycolysis; this is gluconeogenesis.
Stage 2: pyruvic acid oxidation

Pyruvic acid does not take part directly in the Krebs cycle; it goes through three changes first. A molecule of carbon dioxide is removed from pyruvic acid, which becomes acetaldehyde. Acetaldehyde is oxidised (hydrogen removed) to an acetyl group, and a molecule of NAD+ is reduced to NADH. The acetyl group combines with coenzyme A (CoA) to form acetyl-CoA.

blocks.title: Carbon dioxide before oxygen
blocks.text: The release of carbon dioxide takes place before oxygen is involved. So it is not true to say that respiration turns oxygen into carbon dioxide; it is more correct to say that respiration turns glucose into carbon dioxide, and oxygen into water.
Stage 3: Krebs cycle

Acetyl-CoA now enters a cyclic series of reactions in which oxidation is completed. Much of this cycle was worked out by the British biochemist Sir Hans Krebs, so it is the Krebs cycle; it is also called the citric acid cycle, after the six-carbon citric acid formed in its first step. All its steps occur in the mitochondria.

items: Acetyl-CoA splits into CoA and an acetyl group. The acetyl group combines with the four-carbon oxaloacetic acid to form six-carbon citric acid.
Citric acid undergoes oxidative decarboxylation: it is decarboxylated (releasing CO2) and oxidised (reducing NAD+ to NADH), forming the five-carbon alpha-ketoglutaric acid.
Alpha-ketoglutaric acid undergoes further oxidation and decarboxylation, giving the four-carbon succinic acid, which joins CoA to make succinyl-CoA.
The bond between succinic acid and CoA is a high-energy linkage. It splits again into CoA and succinic acid, and the energy released is used to make a molecule of ATP.

Succinic acid is oxidised to fumaric acid. The free energy released when its two hydrogen atoms are removed is not enough to reduce NAD+, so a different electron acceptor, the coenzyme flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), is used and reduced to FADH2.
To regenerate oxaloacetic acid, a molecule of water is added to fumaric acid, which becomes malic acid.
Malic acid is oxidised to oxaloacetic acid; the hydrogen and electrons released convert NAD+ to NADH. This completes the cycle, and oxaloacetic acid is free to bind another acetyl-CoA.

blocks.alt: A strip across the top turns pyruvic acid into acetaldehyde (CO2 out), an acetyl group (NAD+ to NADH) and acetyl-CoA. Below, a circle of seven boxes: citric acid, alpha-ketoglutaric acid, succinyl-CoA, succinic acid, fumaric acid, malic acid and oxaloacetic acid, with the CO2, NADH, FADH2, ATP and water of each step written beside the arrows.
blocks.caption: Pyruvic acid oxidation and the Krebs cycle (original diagram after Figures 5.16 and 5.17 of the chapter).
blocks.long_description: Pyruvic acid loses CO2 to become acetaldehyde, is oxidised to an acetyl group with NAD+ reduced to NADH, and joins coenzyme A as acetyl-CoA. In the cycle the acetyl group joins oxaloacetic acid to make citric acid; two oxidative decarboxylations release two CO2 and make two NADH on the way to succinyl-CoA; splitting the CoA bond makes ATP; succinic acid is oxidised to fumaric acid with FAD reduced to FADH2; water is added to make malic acid; and malic acid is oxidised to oxaloacetic acid with a third NADH, ready for the next acetyl-CoA.

blocks.title: NAD and FAD
blocks.text: In redox reactions, electrons and hydrogen ions are removed from substrates and transferred to the coenzymes NAD+ and FAD, which carry them to the electron transport chain.
Stage 4: electron transport chain and chemiosmosis

In the electron transport chain the electrons are transferred from the reduced coenzymes NADH and FADH2 to a series of electron carriers and finally to oxygen. After getting the electrons, the oxygen attaches to hydrogen ions and forms water. The transfer along the carriers is a series of oxidations and reductions: a carrier is oxidised when it loses electrons and the next is reduced when it gains them. The electrons lose energy during this carrier-to-carrier transport, and chemiosmosis is the mechanism by which membranes couple these redox reactions to the synthesis of ATP.

Pathway of electrons: the respiratory electron transport chain is built into the inner membrane of the mitochondrion. At the start, NADH is oxidised and its electrons are taken up by coenzyme Q; if FADH2 is oxidised, its electrons also go to coenzyme Q. Reduced CoQ transports the electrons to cytochrome b, which passes them to cytochrome c, which passes them to the cytochrome a complex (a complex of two cytochromes), which transports them to an atom of oxygen at the bottom end of the chain.

Synthesis of ATP: as the redox reactions occur, the energy released from the electrons is used for the active transport of H+ ions from the matrix of the mitochondrion across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space, so many H+ ions are deposited there. The resulting H+ gradient stores potential energy. The H+ ions diffuse back along their gradient from the intermembrane space into the matrix through the protein ATP synthase, and as they pass, their flow drives the synthesis of ATP. The oxidation of one NADH in the chain produces three ATP, and the oxidation of one FADH2 produces two ATP. At the end, two hydrogen ions are taken by the oxygen atom, which has also taken two electrons, to form water.

blocks.alt: The inner mitochondrial membrane in cross-section with CoQ, cytochrome b, cytochrome c and the cytochrome a complex in a row, and ATP synthase at the right. NADH and FADH2 feed electrons in at CoQ; red H+ arrows are pumped up into the intermembrane space; oxygen and H+ below the last carrier form water; H+ flows back down through ATP synthase, turning ADP and Pi into ATP.
blocks.caption: The electron transport chain and chemiosmosis in the mitochondrion (original diagram after Figures 5.18 and 5.19 of the chapter).
blocks.long_description: NADH and FADH2 give their electrons to coenzyme Q; the electrons pass to cytochrome b, cytochrome c and the cytochrome a complex, each carrier being reduced and then oxidised, and finally to oxygen, which takes two H+ to form water. The energy the electrons lose pumps H+ from the matrix into the intermembrane space. The H+ gradient drives H+ back through ATP synthase, which makes ATP: three per NADH and two per FADH2.

blocks.text: Substrate-level phosphorylation

Cells generate ATP by phosphorylation, adding a phosphate group to ADP, in two ways: chemiosmotic phosphorylation (chemiosmosis) and substrate-level phosphorylation. Substrate-level phosphorylation is much simpler and involves no membrane or electron transport chain: an enzyme transfers a phosphate group from an organic substrate molecule to ADP, giving a new organic molecule and ATP. In the last step of glycolysis, for example, an enzyme transfers the phosphate of phosphoenol pyruvic acid (PEP) to ADP, so ADP becomes ATP and PEP becomes pyruvic acid. It accounts for only a small percentage of the ATP a cell generates.
Overview of the energy extracted from the oxidation of glucose

The NADH and FADH2 produced in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle pass their energy-rich electrons to the electron transport chain, where ATP is produced. Each NADH generated in the Krebs cycle gives three ATP by chemiosmosis. Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm, and the NADH it produces must be transported across the mitochondrial membrane, at a cost of one ATP per NADH, so each NADH of glycolysis produces two ATP in the final balance sheet instead of three. Each FADH2 leads to two ATP. In this way the aerobic oxidation of glucose yields a net profit of 36 ATP, while the glycolysis of anaerobic oxidation gives only 2; aerobic oxidation is 18 times more efficient.

blocks.alt: Four stage boxes in a row, glycolysis, pyruvic acid oxidation, Krebs cycle and electron transport, with their ATP, NADH and FADH2 yields beneath, and a table adding the ATP from each source to a net total of 36.
blocks.caption: The energy extracted from the aerobic oxidation of one glucose (original diagram after Figure 5.20 of the chapter).
blocks.long_description: Glycolysis gives 2 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and 2 NADH worth 2 ATP each after the cost of entering the mitochondrion. Pyruvic acid oxidation gives 2 NADH worth 3 ATP each. The Krebs cycle gives 2 ATP, 6 NADH worth 3 ATP each and 2 FADH2 worth 2 ATP each. The total is 36 ATP, against 2 ATP from anaerobic respiration, so aerobic respiration is 18 times more efficient.

blocks.caption: ATP from one glucose in aerobic respiration
rows: 2 NADH from glycolysis (2 each after transport cost)
2 NADH from pyruvic acid oxidation (3 each)
6 NADH from the Krebs cycle (3 each)
2 FADH2 from the Krebs cycle (2 each)

blocks.text: Other organic molecules as fuel

Free glucose molecules are not common in our diet; we consume sucrose and other disaccharides, starch, fats and proteins. Proteins may be used as fuel but must first be digested to their amino acids. Typically a cell uses most amino acids to make its own proteins; some are de-aminated (the amino group detached) and converted into other organic compounds, usually pyruvic acid, acetyl-CoA or the organic acids of the Krebs cycle, and their energy is converted to ATP. Lipids are excellent cellular fuel because they contain many carbon-hydrogen bonds. They are first hydrolysed into glycerol and fatty acids; glycerol is converted to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, an intermediate of glycolysis, while the fatty acids are changed into acetyl-CoA. In this way both enter cellular respiration.

blocks.prompt: A sprinter's muscles switch to lactic acid fermentation during a race. Explain why this is worth doing even though it yields only 2 ATP per glucose, and why aerobic respiration gives 36.
blocks.explanation: Fermentation reduces pyruvic acid with NADH, regenerating the NAD+ that glycolysis needs, so glycolysis can keep making ATP quickly when oxygen cannot reach the muscle fast enough. Aerobic respiration oxidises glucose completely: pyruvic acid oxidation and the Krebs cycle load 10 NADH and 2 FADH2, and the electron transport chain with chemiosmosis converts these into about 32 more ATP, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor.

blocks.text: Quick recap

items: C6H12O6 + 6O2 gives 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy; glucose is the respiratory fuel. Anaerobic respiration (fermentation) gives 2 ATP: alcoholic (ethanol + CO2; bacteria, yeast) or lactic acid (muscle, bacteria).
Aerobic respiration has four stages. Glycolysis (cytosol, no oxygen): preparatory phase spends 2 ATP to split glucose into 2 G3P; oxidative phase gives 2 NADH and 4 ATP, ending in 2 pyruvic acid.

Pyruvic acid oxidation: CO2 removed, NAD+ reduced, acetyl group joins CoA. Krebs cycle (mitochondria; Sir Hans Krebs): citric acid, alpha-ketoglutaric, succinyl-CoA, succinic, fumaric, malic, oxaloacetic; per turn 2 CO2, 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 ATP.

Electron transport chain (inner membrane): NADH and FADH2 to CoQ, cytochromes b, c and a, to oxygen (water). Chemiosmosis pumps H+ into the intermembrane space and ATP synthase makes ATP: 3 per NADH, 2 per FADH2. Substrate-level phosphorylation moves a phosphate from a substrate (PEP) to ADP.
Net 36 ATP per glucose aerobically against 2 anaerobically (18 times). Proteins (as amino acids) and lipids (glycerol to G3P, fatty acids to acetyl-CoA) also feed respiration.
